newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-French single currency efforts get EU boost.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French single currency efforts get EU boost.

text.p: France's efforts to qualify for monetary union received a boost on Thursday when the European Commission said it accepted a plan to use 37.5 billion francs ($7.35 billion) in pension funds to cut the 1997 budget deficit.
The approval sparked some fears that other European Union countries struggling to meet tough criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU) would be tempted to take similar steps.

"I think it is wrong ... It challenges other countries which seemingly do not fulfil the criteria to take similar measures," German Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher told reporters in Hamburg.

The head of the Commission's statistics office Eurostat authorised the plan to transfer the funds from state-owned France Telecom to the budget, despite reports that German, British and Dutch experts had opposed the move.
Eurostat Director-General Yves Franchet was responsible for the technical assessment of whether the French plan was in line with agreed European Union accounting rules.
"Clearly it will encourage others to try the same thing," said senior economist Don Eggington at Daiwa Institute of Research in London.
But international economist Ian Gunner at Chase Investment Bank said "fortunately many countries have already formed their budgets ...like Portugal, Spain and Italy."
As monetary union without France was inconceivable, Daiwa's Eggington said the Eurostat decision had boosted the chances of the project becoming a reality.
"At the end of the day whether it is good or not depends on your view whether EMU is good or not for Europe," he said.
Explaining the decision, Commission spokesman Patrick Child said the French money move was seen as a capital and not a financial transfer, "which means they are in the clear".
The announcement came only two days after reports that an advisory EU accounting committee had not been able to approve the payment, causing the franc to fall against the German mark.
After Thursday's announcement, the franc firmed slightly, ending at 3.3760/55 against the mark versus 3.3785/90.

At issue was whether the transfer of money to cover future pension liabilities could be used by the French government in its accounting to reduce its 1997 deficit to meet one of the Maastricht treaty criteria for monetary union in 1999.
Critics have said the transfer smacked of creative accounting and ran counter to EU guidelines for countries to take sustainable economic measures to qualify for EMU.
EU officials estimate that it will help reduce the French deficit by between 0.4 and 0.5 percent of GDP.
Child said a small minority of the representatives of member states and of the central banks on the committee had "expressed doubts about the approach proposed by the French."
He did not name the sceptical countries, but an EU source said on Wednesday that German, British and Dutch officials had argued against allowing France to use the transfer.
The conclusion that Eurostat's Franchet had drawn from the consultations was that "a large majority of participants were able to accept the French approach," Child said.
Asked whether other EU countries could do similar accounting exercises, he said all cases would be examined on their merits.
"Clearly there is no discrimination...so in identical circumstances in another country it would seem to me logical that the same result would be achieved," Child added.
Various countries have been accused by economists of window-dressing to cut budget deficits in 1997, the year on which eligibility for membership will be judged.
Gunner at Chase predicted that the Eurostat decision would lead to further discontent among German officials.
However, he noted that German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, deeply committed to monetary union, had avoided criticising the plan. (1$=5.1 francs)
